26 min read
Just now

--

In which the author says a sentence out loud, hears how it sounds, and then spends an unreasonable number of sections establishing that the correct response to it is not grief, not panic, and — most disappointingly for everyone involved — not even a decent existential crisis. Let’s call it simply: “A Farewell to Arms, Filed Without Regret”…
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…tinkering around, nobody checking…I said it to a friend, late, in the tone men our age use instead of therapy: I’m not a programmer anymore.
And I heard, immediately, what it sounded like. Not a career announcement. Not a complaint. It sounded like a man in a bar telling you, with a small and not entirely unhappy smile, that he used to be a partisan. That there was a forest once, and a unit, and things that mattered enormously at the time. That nobody has needed any of it for years — and that the forest, incidentally, is a housing estate now, and the estate is perfectly nice, and his grandchildren live in it.
That’s the register. A farewell to arms, without a bugle, without a pension, and — this is the part that surprised me most — without regret. What follows is my working.

I. The Sentence, Unpacked
“The unexamined life is not worth living.”
— Socrates, who never had to fill in a timesheet
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…the day’s work, itemised, suspiciously typing-free…Here’s what an ordinary working day looks like now. Audit your own against it; I’ll wait.
I described what a system needed to do. I corrected a misunderstanding about its behaviour at the edges. I said the same thing again in smaller words, because the first version had been too clever and had produced something confident and wrong. I decided — and this was the only irreplaceable act of the day — that one particular behaviour was diplomatically convenient and factually dishonest, and that we’d be doing the honest one anyway. Then I checked the result and found the place where the machine had invented a requirement nobody had asked for, with the serene confidence of a man in a pub explaining the offside rule.
Shipped. Worked. And not one minute of it was programming in the sense I spent two decades learning.
Show me that day twenty years ago, and I’d have called it the job of a business analyst, in the tone one reserves for describing a cousin’s career in insurance. Today it’s the part of the work nobody else in the building can do, and the near-total absence of typing has stopped registering as a demotion. That journey — from insult to job description — is the entire story. Everything below is me trying to be honest about it while remaining, at all times, insufferable.

II. Not Destroyed. Declassified.
“I’m not dead yet! I think I’ll go for a walk!”
— Monty Python and the Holy Grail, on the state of the profession
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…the cart, the corpse, the walk & “not quite dead, yet”…Our industry’s argument about all this is stuck on the wrong verb. Everyone wants to know whether programming has been destroyed — killed, replaced, made obsolete, whichever apocalypse fits the headline and the funding round. It’s the wrong question, and it produces two equally tiresome camps: the mourners, who are grieving a corpse that keeps insisting it’s not dead yet and would quite like to go for a walk; and the salesmen, who are cheerfully loading it onto the cart anyway because they’re paid by the body.
The accurate verb is quieter and much less marketable. Programming stopped being the problem.
Not a problem. The problem — the one that required a heroic solution. For most of my working life, the central difficulty in getting software to exist was the making of it: the months of construction, the artisanal maintenance afterwards, the accumulated skill needed to persuade a machine to do a moderately complicated thing without lying about it. That was the bottleneck. Everything else — the salaries, the mythology, the conference circuit, the job titles, the entire flattering self-image of my profession — was scaffolding erected around that single hard fact.
The hard fact has moved. Not vanished; moved. Construction became cheap enough that the difficulty relocated upward into the questions surrounding it: what should exist, why, who’s accountable, what happens when it’s wrong, and what precisely the business means by that word it keeps using in meetings as though everyone agrees on it.
Which is a demotion for the craft and a promotion for the judgment. I notice that the people most upset about this are, overwhelmingly, the ones who preferred the craft. Understandable. It was the fun part. It was also — and I say this with love, at this hour, among friends — the part most amenable to being performed by something that doesn’t require lunch, sleep, or a difficult conversation about its title.

III. The Cobbler’s Queue
“The shoemaker’s children go barefoot.”
— proverb, several nations, all of them correct
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…church shoes, carried, not worn…Here’s the analogy that finally settled it for me. Three acts, and the third is where we live.
Act one…
A pair of shoes was once a problem. It required a craftsman, an apprenticeship, tools, hides, and years of skill you couldn’t fake. You joined a queue measured in seasons. You paid a serious fraction of a year’s earnings. And the resulting shoes were so valuable that people walked to church barefoot and put them on at the door, because ruining them was not a recoverable event, and because God, being reasonable, could see the shoes were in your hand.
Act two…
Shoes stopped being a problem, and the problem became getting yourself to the shopping centre to see whether they’re on sale. Same object; entirely different difficulty. The craft hadn’t disappeared — it had emigrated into a factory and then onto a container ship, and human effort had migrated from manufacture to selection.
Act three…
Now it’s whatever arrives from a website, and if the sole detaches there’s tape and a shrug. Nobody’s grandchildren will be told about these shoes. Nobody will walk anywhere barefoot on their account.
And here’s the part the mourners skip and the salesmen never mention: the cobbler still exists. Bespoke shoemakers are alive, magnificent, booked out for months, and serve enthusiasts, luxury buyers, and people with difficult feet. The trade didn’t die. It stopped being the way shoes happen and became a boutique on a street where everybody else buys online.
That’s not a tragedy. That’s a change of address, and the postal service has been fully informed. Now substitute “software” for “shoes” throughout, including the bit about God being reasonable, and you have my thesis.

IV. Heroism Was a Price, Not a Virtue
“We few, we happy few.”
— Shakespeare, on a project that shipped a year late and changed everyone involved
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…the bridge, defended, subsequently demolished for a car park…Every senior engineer has a campaign. The application that consumed a large team for the better part of a year, argued over in rooms with whiteboards, defended in review with the intensity of men defending a bridge, and leaving behind a bond that no corporate away-day has ever successfully manufactured. We speak of these with reverence. The reverence is real, and I’m not here to sneer at it — I have mine, and I’d bore you with it given the smallest opening and a second drink.
But here’s the arithmetic nobody does out loud. That project didn’t take a year and a small army because the problem required a year and a small army. It took that because the tools of the era charged that much. The heroism was the invoice, not the achievement.
Which is why today’s version of the same conversation — “could you just generate that by Friday? it’s only meant to be a demo” — is not the insult it feels like. It stings, certainly. It stings because it revalues the currency our self-respect was denominated in, and nobody enjoys waking up to find their savings redenominated overnight by a central bank they didn’t vote for. But the request is usually correct. It really is a demo. It really can be done by Friday. What changed isn’t the significance of the work; it’s the price of the labour — and we had been quietly conflating the two for about thirty years, the way one conflates the cost of a wedding with the quality of a marriage.
I mourn the campaigns a bit. I would be lying if I said I want the invoice reissued.

V. The Milk Is Spilled
“It is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future.”
— attributed to everyone; correct regardless
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…the milk, the floor, the futility…Now the argument I’d defend in a hostile room, because it makes most of the industry’s current shouting irrelevant.
Everybody is litigating the bubble. Will it pop; will the big labs survive; will the valuations turn out to have been blockchain in a better suit; will some smaller outfit somewhere quietly eat everyone’s lunch and then their pension. My answer to all of it: it does not matter, because the milk is already spilt.
Note what this argument doesn’t require. It doesn’t require any lab to survive. It doesn’t require scaling to continue, valuations to make sense, or agents to achieve enlightenment. It requires only what is already true on an ordinary evening: an over-trained open-weights model, a decent laptop, a network connection — and you can knock out a serious slab of scaffolding in a few hours. Better than a competent team of my generation managed in a month of not sleeping. With tests. And with documentation, which — I feel obliged to note — that team did not produce, because at 3 AM documentation is what you solemnly promise to do next sprint, in the same voice you use for the gym.
You cannot un-ring that. If the entire commercial edifice collapsed on a Wednesday, then on Thursday I could still describe a system to a machine and receive a working sketch of it. The capability has left the boardroom and moved into the spare room, where it sits next to the exercise bike, being used considerably more often.
So the bubble debate is a debate about the weather over an industry’s share price. It is not a debate about the trade. The trade already changed — quietly, without a press release, at some point while we were all still arguing about whether it would.

VI. So It Goes
“DON’T THINK OF IT AS DYING, said Death. JUST THINK OF IT AS LEAVING EARLY TO AVOID THE RUSH.”
— Terry Pratchett (with Neil Gaiman, who will want that noted), Good Omens — kinder about it than the industry manages
Press enter or click to view image in full size

…the hourglass, the spreadsheet, the queue…I’d like to hold a small funeral now, because I’ve noticed that our profession has no rites, and a trade without rites is a trade that processes its grief in Slack, badly, at length, in threads.
So, in the manner of Vonnegut, who understood that the only dignified way to record a death is briefly:
The junior who learned the framework everyone agreed was the future, and who is now the only person alive who remembers its lifecycle hooks. So it goes.
The architecture I defended for three weeks, which was correct, which won, and which was deleted eleven months later by a man who had not been born when the argument started. So it goes.
The certification. So it goes.
The build tool that was going to end build tools. So it goes. Its successor, currently in beta, currently perfect, currently the last one we’ll ever need. So it goes.
The version of me who could hold an entire system in his head at once, and who was insufferable about it, and who was — this is the part I mind — actually right that it mattered. So it goes.
The other version of me, some years later, who learned to stop holding it all and trust the tests instead, and who was also right, and who is also gone. So it goes.
The evenings. Genuinely
